---
title: "Nonuniform grids"
engine: julia
---

```{julia}
#| echo: false
using ConvolutionInterpolations, CairoMakie, Printf
```

On a uniform grid every kernel copy is the same polynomial, shifted. On a nonuniform grid the
spacing changes from interval to interval, and the Julia package carries a second family of
kernels whose polynomial pieces are recomputed for the actual knots, so that the interpolant
keeps its cardinality and its polynomial reproduction on any strictly increasing knot vector.
Nothing needs to be switched on: passing knots that are not uniformly spaced selects them.

The Python port works on uniform grids only, so far; the [feature matrix](../features.qmd)
tracks the port.

## The kernels

Three kinds of kernel work on a nonuniform grid:

- `:b5` to `:b13` are the nonuniform counterparts of the high-order kernels. They converge at
  order degree + 1, so `:b5` at 6th order and `:b13` at 14th, and they provide derivatives up
  to order degree − 2, the last continuous one: 3 for `:b5`, 5 for `:b7`, and so on up to 11
  for `:b13`. Their weights are projected onto each interval in exact rational arithmetic when
  the interpolant is built, so construction costs one projection per interval and grows with
  the number of intervals; evaluation is as local as on a uniform grid.
- `:n3` is the nonuniform cubic, the counterpart of `:a3`: closed-form weights, a four-wide
  stencil and no precomputation, so it costs about what the uniform cubic costs. It
  interpolates only; derivatives need a `:b` kernel. The two names are interchangeable, and
  the grid decides which form is used.
- `:a0` and `:a1`, nearest-neighbour and linear interpolation, work on any grid.

A grid with a nonuniform axis uses either `:b` kernels on every axis, which may differ from
axis to axis, or one of the other kernels on all axes. The default is the same as on a uniform
grid up to three dimensions, `:b7` in one and two and `:b5` in three; from four dimensions it
is `:n3`, where a uniform grid uses `:a4`. The other `:a` kernels, `:a4`, `:a5` and `:a7`, are
for uniform grids only.

## A first example

A damped sine sampled on a grid that is dense where the function varies fast and sparse where
it has settled, interpolated with `:b7` and differentiated twice:

```{julia}
x = [0.0, 0.15, 0.4, 0.7, 1.5, 2.5, 3.8, 4.2, 4.6, 4.8, 5.0,
     5.3, 5.6, 6.0, 6.5, 7.0, 7.3, 7.8, 8.2, 8.5, 9.0, 9.5, 10.0]   # an irregular knot vector
f(x) = sin(x) * exp(-x / 5)                               # the function being sampled
y = f.(x)                                                 # the values at the knots

itp = convolution_interpolation(x, y; kernel = :b7)       # nonuniform grid detected from the knots
d1 = convolution_interpolation(x, y; kernel = :b7, derivative = 1)   # its first derivative
d2 = convolution_interpolation(x, y; kernel = :b7, derivative = 2)   # its second derivative

xf = range(0, 10, length = 600)                           # fine points for plotting
fig = Figure(size = (800, 400))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "x")
lines!(ax, xf, itp.(xf); label = "interpolant")
lines!(ax, xf, d1.(xf); label = "first derivative")
lines!(ax, xf, d2.(xf); label = "second derivative")
lines!(ax, xf, f.(xf); color = :black, label = "f")
scatter!(ax, x, y; markersize = 10, color = :white, strokecolor = :black, strokewidth = 1.5, label = "knots")
Legend(fig[1, 2], ax)
fig
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
df(x) = exp(-x / 5) * (cos(x) - sin(x) / 5)               # the exact first derivative
println("| at x = 2.9 (a sparse part of the grid) | f | f′ |")
println("|:--|--:|--:|")
@printf("| interpolant | %.10f | %.10f |\n", itp(2.9), d1(2.9))
@printf("| exact | %.10f | %.10f |\n", f(2.9), df(2.9))
```

## Convergence on a graded grid

The orders hold on nonuniform grids as they do on uniform ones. Here the knots are a uniform
grid pushed through a smooth monotone map, so that each refinement keeps the grading and halves
every spacing, and Runge's function is interpolated with four kernels:

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "The convergence study"
runge(x) = 1 / (1 + 25x^2)                                # Runge's function
grade(u) = u + 0.3 * sin(π * u) / π                       # a monotone map of [−1, 1] onto itself, dense near the centre
xr = range(-1, 1, length = 2001)                          # fine points for measuring the error
kernels = (:n3, :b5, :b7, :b9, :b11)
ns = [41, 81, 161, 321, 641]                              # the numbers of knots
hs = 2 ./ (ns .- 1)                                       # the spacings of the uniform grid before grading

errors = [begin
              xn = grade.(range(-1, 1, length = n))       # the graded knots
              itp_k = convolution_interpolation(xn, runge.(xn); kernel = k)
              maximum(abs.(itp_k.(xr) .- runge.(xr)))
          end for n in ns, k in kernels]

fig = Figure(size = (800, 420))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xscale = log10, yscale = log10, xreversed = true,
          xlabel = "mean spacing h", ylabel = "largest error")
for (j, k) in enumerate(kernels)
    scatterlines!(ax, hs, max.(errors[:, j], 1e-17); markersize = 8, label = string(k))
end
Legend(fig[1, 2], ax)
fig
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
observed = [begin
                e = errors[:, j]
                i = findlast(v -> v > 1e-11, e); i = max(i, 2)   # the finest grid still clear of rounding
                log(e[i-1] / e[i]) / log(hs[i-1] / hs[i])
            end for j in eachindex(kernels)]
println("| | ", join(("`$k`" for k in kernels), " | "), " |")
println("|:--|", "--:|"^length(kernels))
println("| observed convergence order | ", join((@sprintf("%.2f", o) for o in observed), " | "), " |")
```

## In more dimensions

Nonuniform knots can be given per axis, and the grid is the tensor product of the axes, so a
log-spaced axis and a uniform axis combine freely. Each axis chooses its own kernel and
derivative order:

```{julia}
xg = 10 .^ range(-2, 0, length = 25)                      # a log-spaced axis on [0.01, 1]
yg = range(0, 1, length = 20)                             # a uniform axis
data = [log(xi) * cos(π * yi) for xi in xg, yi in yg]     # log(x)·cos(πy) on the grid

itp2 = convolution_interpolation((xg, yg), data; kernel = :b7)                       # interpolation
dx2 = convolution_interpolation((xg, yg), data; kernel = (:b7, :b5), derivative = (1, 0))  # ∂/∂x, two kernels

itp2(0.05, 0.3), dx2(0.05, 0.3)
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
println("| at (0.05, 0.3) | f | ∂f/∂x |")
println("|:--|--:|--:|")
@printf("| interpolant | %.10f | %.10f |\n", itp2(0.05, 0.3), dx2(0.05, 0.3))
@printf("| exact | %.10f | %.10f |\n", log(0.05) * cos(0.3π), cos(0.3π) / 0.05)
```

The precomputation of the `:b` kernels is per interval and per axis, so it stays cheap on a
tensor-product grid: a 1000 × 1000 grid needs two thousand projections, not a million.

## Targeted refinement

Because the `:b` weights belong to the intervals, a nonuniform grid can be refined in place.
`convolution_suggest` estimates the error of a one-dimensional `:b` interpolant interval by
interval, from the knots and values alone, and returns the midpoints of the intervals where
the estimate exceeds `tol`, a fraction of the range of the data. `convolution_refine` takes
those points and the data there and returns the interpolant on the merged knots. It computes
only the weights that the new knots touch: an interval keeps its weights unless one of the M
knots on either side of it is new, with M = 5 for `:b5` up to 9 for `:b13`, so the cost of a
new knot does not grow with the grid.

Runge's function on a coarse irregular grid with `:b13`, refined by repeating the two until
nothing is suggested, and for comparison by adding the midpoint of every interval at each
pass, until that run is as accurate:

```{julia}
x0 = [-1.0, -0.86, -0.71, -0.58, -0.44, -0.33, -0.21, -0.1, 0.0,
      0.12, 0.22, 0.35, 0.47, 0.6, 0.73, 0.87, 1.0]       # a coarse irregular knot vector
maxerr(f, itp, xs) = maximum(abs, itp.(xs) .- f.(xs))     # the largest error of itp at xs
itp0 = convolution_interpolation(x0, runge.(x0); kernel = :b13)  # the coarse interpolant

# refine where convolution_suggest estimates the error above tol, until nothing is
# suggested or the passes run out; returns the interpolant, its knots, and the knot count
# and the largest error at xs after each pass
function refine_targeted(f, itp, x, xs; tol = 1e-6, passes = 30)
    counts, errs = [length(x)], [maxerr(f, itp, xs)]      # the state before refining
    for pass in 1:passes                                  # a limit on the passes
        x_new = convolution_suggest(itp; tol)             # midpoints of intervals above tol
        isempty(x_new) && break                           # the estimate is below tol everywhere
        itp = convolution_refine(itp, x_new, f.(x_new))   # knots added there
        x = sort(vcat(x, x_new))                          # the knots of the refined interpolant
        push!(counts, length(x))                          # its knot count
        push!(errs, maxerr(f, itp, xs))                   # and its error
    end
    return itp, x, counts, errs
end

# add the midpoint of every interval at each pass, until the largest error at xs is at most
# target or the passes run out; returns the same as refine_targeted
function refine_everywhere(f, itp, x, xs, target; passes = 8)
    counts, errs = [length(x)], [maxerr(f, itp, xs)]      # the state before refining
    for pass in 1:passes                                  # a limit, as each pass doubles the knots
        last(errs) <= target && break                     # as accurate as the target
        x_new = (x[1:end-1] .+ x[2:end]) ./ 2             # the midpoint of every interval
        itp = convolution_refine(itp, x_new, f.(x_new))   # knots added everywhere
        x = sort(vcat(x, x_new))                          # the knots of the refined interpolant
        push!(counts, length(x))                          # its knot count
        push!(errs, maxerr(f, itp, xs))                   # and its error
    end
    return itp, x, counts, errs
end

itp_t, x_t, counts_t, errs_t = refine_targeted(runge, itp0, x0, xr)               # targeted run
itp_u, x_u, counts_u, errs_u = refine_everywhere(runge, itp0, x0, xr, last(errs_t))  # untargeted

x_added = setdiff(x_t, x0)                                # the knots the targeted run added
knot_style = (markersize = 10, color = :white, strokecolor = :black, strokewidth = 1.5)
fig = Figure(size = (800, 750))
ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "x", title = "coarse, $(length(x0)) knots")
ax2 = Axis(fig[1, 2]; xlabel = "x", title = "refined, $(length(x_t)) knots")
for (ax, itp) in ((ax1, itp0), (ax2, itp_t))              # each panel: interpolant over f
    lines!(ax, xr, itp.(xr); label = "interpolant")
    lines!(ax, xr, runge.(xr); color = :black, linestyle = :dash, label = "f")
    scatter!(ax, x0, runge.(x0); knot_style..., label = "initial knots")
end
scatter!(ax2, x_added, runge.(x_added); markersize = 6, color = :black, label = "added knots")
Legend(fig[2, 1:2], ax2; orientation = :horizontal)       # one legend for both panels
ax3 = Axis(fig[3, 1:2]; xlabel = "knots", ylabel = "largest error", yscale = log10)
scatterlines!(ax3, counts_t, errs_t; label = "targeted")
scatterlines!(ax3, counts_u, errs_u; label = "every interval halved")
Legend(fig[4, 1:2], ax3; orientation = :horizontal)
fig
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
println("| | knots | largest error |")
println("|:--|--:|--:|")
@printf("| coarse | %d | %.1e |\n", first(counts_t), first(errs_t))
@printf("| targeted | %d | %.1e |\n", last(counts_t), last(errs_t))
@printf("| every interval halved | %d | %.1e |\n", last(counts_u), last(errs_u))
```

Where the coarse interpolant overshoots, the estimate is large, and the targeted run adds its
knots there; halving every interval also spends knots where the interpolant was already
accurate. The table shows what each run needs for the same accuracy.

The estimate sees only the knots and their values. A feature that lies entirely between two
knots is invisible to it, and where the data have a kink or a jump the estimate does not fall,
so the same interval is suggested at every pass: a refinement loop needs a limit on its passes,
as above. A tolerance near the precision of the data flags intervals without end, since the
differences are then rounding noise.

Adding one knot to a grid of two thousand, against rebuilding the interpolant on the merged
knots:

```{julia}
using Chairmarks
xb = sinpi.(range(-0.5, 0.5, length = 2000))              # 2000 knots, dense at the ends
itp_b = convolution_interpolation(xb, runge.(xb); kernel = :b13)  # the interpolant on them
x1 = (xb[1000] + xb[1001]) / 2                            # one new knot, in the middle
xm = sort(vcat(xb, x1))                                   # the merged knots

itp_r = convolution_refine(itp_b, [x1], runge.([x1]))     # the refined interpolant, and the
                                                          # warm-up of its timing below
itp_m = convolution_interpolation(xm, runge.(xm); kernel = :b13)  # the rebuilt one, likewise
t_refine = (@b convolution_refine(itp_b, [x1], runge.([x1]))).time                # adding the knot
t_build = (@b convolution_interpolation(xm, runge.(xm); kernel = :b13)).time      # rebuilding
diff_rm = maximum(abs, itp_r.(xr) .- itp_m.(xr));         # their largest difference on [-1, 1]
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
println("| | adding one knot | rebuilding |")
println("|:--|--:|--:|")
@printf("| time (ms) | %.3f | %.3f |\n", 1e3 * t_refine, 1e3 * t_build)
println()
@printf("The two interpolants differ by at most %.1e on [-1, 1].\n", diff_rm)
```

## What is not available

A nonuniform interpolant has no antiderivative of its own: a negative `derivative` needs a
uniform grid. There are two ways to integrate data on a nonuniform grid, and which one fits
depends on the data. For trusted data, evaluate the nonuniform interpolant on a uniform grid
fine enough to carry it, and integrate that with `derivative = -1`, as on the
[integrals page](integrals.qmd); this keeps the order of the nonuniform kernel. For noisy
data, or data that are not on a grid at all, the [scattered-data fit](scattered.qmd) returns
an interpolant on a uniform grid directly, smoothed by default, and that interpolant takes a
negative `derivative` like any other.

Lazy construction is not available on a nonuniform grid: the ghost values are built when the
interpolant is created, and asking for `lazy = true` is an error.
